course.name: Statistics for Economists
course.tagline: Distributions, the CLT, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests.

cards.simple: x̄ = (1/n) Σ x<sub>i</sub>. The balance point of the data. Pulled toward outliers.
more: In a right-skewed distribution (like income) the mean is above the median.

cards.simple: The middle value of the sorted data (the average of the two middle values when n is even). Resistant to outliers.
s² = Σ(x<sub>i</sub> − x̄)² / (n − 1). Dividing by n − 1 makes s² an unbiased estimator of σ².
more: n − 1 = degrees of freedom: once x̄ is fixed, only n − 1 deviations are free.

cards.simple: z = (x − μ)/σ: how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean.
IQR = Q3 − Q1. Points below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR are flagged as outliers.
r = Cov(x, y)/(sx sy), between −1 and 1. Measures linear association only, and correlation ≠ causation.
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B): the probability of A once you know B happened.
A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B), equivalently P(A | B) = P(A).
P(A | B) = P(B | A)·P(A) / P(B), with P(B) = P(B|A)P(A) + P(B|A<sup>c</sup>)P(A<sup>c</sup>).
more: Rare conditions + imperfect tests ⇒ most positives can be false positives (base-rate fallacy).

cards.simple: E[X] = Σ x·P(X = x) (discrete) or ∫ x f(x) dx (continuous). Linear: E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b.
Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X). Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X, Y), so the covariance term drops out when X and Y are independent.
Number of successes in n independent trials with success probability p. P(X = k) = C(n,k) p<sup>k</sup>(1−p)<sup>n−k</sup>. Mean np, variance np(1−p).
Counts of events in a fixed interval at constant rate λ. P(X = k) = e<sup>−λ</sup>λ<sup>k</sup>/k!. Mean = variance = λ.
Bell-shaped, symmetric, described by μ and σ. About 68% / 95% / 99.7% of values lie within 1 / 2 / 3 σ of μ.
Like the standard normal but with fatter tails. Used when σ is estimated by s. Approaches N(0,1) as df → ∞.
more: One-sample t: df = n − 1. Two-sided 95% critical value: 2.262 at df 9, 2.042 at df 30, 1.96 in the limit.

cards.simple: Sum of k squared independent standard normals. Right-skewed, mean k. Used for variance tests, goodness-of-fit, and independence in contingency tables.
The distribution of a statistic (like x̄) across all possible samples of size n from the population.
SE = σ/√n (estimated by s/√n). Quadrupling n halves the SE.
For large n, x̄ is approximately N(μ, σ²/n) whatever the population’s shape (as long as σ is finite).
more: Rule of thumb n ≥ 30, more for very skewed populations. See the CLT simulator in Tools.

cards.simple: An estimator whose expected value equals the parameter: E[θ̂] = θ. x̄ is unbiased for μ, and s² is unbiased for σ².
An estimator that converges to the true parameter as n → ∞ (its sampling distribution collapses onto θ).
x̄ ± z*·σ/√n (σ known) or x̄ ± t*<sub>n−1</sub>·s/√n (σ unknown).
more: Margin of error grows with confidence level and σ, shrinks with √n.

cards.simple: If we repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of the intervals built this way would contain μ. Any one interval either does or doesn’t.
The probability, assuming H₀ is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not P(H₀ true).

cards.term: Type I and Type II errors
cards.simple: Type I: rejecting a true H₀ (probability α). Type II: failing to reject a false H₀ (probability β).
1 − β: the probability of rejecting H₀ when it is false. Rises with n, effect size and α, and falls with σ.
β̂₁ = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)/Σ(x−x̄)² = Cov(x,y)/Var(x); β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄. Minimizes the sum of squared residuals.
more: With an intercept, residuals sum to zero and the line passes through (x̄, ȳ).

cards.simple: Share of the variance in y explained by the regression: 1 − SSR/SST. In simple regression, R² = r².

options.why: That’s P(X < 130). The question asks for the upper tail.
That’s both tails, P(|Z| > 2). Only the upper tail is asked.
That’s P(Z > 1), as if z were 30/30. The z-score divides by σ = 15.

questions.label: Q2
questions.prompt: n = 36, σ = 12 (known), x̄ = 50. The 95% confidence interval for μ is…

options.why: Used σ instead of the standard error σ/√n.
1.645 × 2 = 3.29 is the 90% margin.
Divided σ by n (12/36) instead of √n.

questions.label: Q3
questions.prompt: A test gives p = 0.03. Which statement is correct?

options.t: If H₀ were true, results at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
options.why: That’s the definition: a probability computed assuming H₀.

options.t: There is a 3% chance H₀ is true
options.why: The p-value assumes H₀. It is not the probability that H₀ is true.

options.t: There is a 97% chance Hₐ is true
options.why: Same error in reverse. Frequentist tests don’t give probabilities of hypotheses.

options.t: The effect is large and important
options.why: A small p can come from a tiny effect with a big n. Significance isn’t importance.

options.t: Rejecting H₀ when it is actually true
options.why: Its probability is the significance level α.

options.t: Failing to reject H₀ when it is false
options.why: That’s a Type II error (probability β).
That’s just a mistake. Type I/II refer to wrong decisions about H₀.

options.t: Rejecting Hₐ when it is true
options.why: We never “reject Hₐ”. We reject or fail to reject H₀.

questions.label: Q5
questions.prompt: Incomes are strongly right-skewed. For samples of n = 200, the sampling distribution of x̄ is…

options.t: Approximately normal, centered at μ with SD σ/√200
options.why: The CLT: x̄ is approximately normal for large n whatever the population’s shape.
Individual incomes are skewed, but averages of 200 are close to normal (the CLT).
Only approximately. Exactly normal requires a normal population.
x̄ is unbiased for the mean μ, not the median.

questions.label: Q6
questions.prompt: To cut the standard error of x̄ in half, the sample size must be…

options.why: Doubling n divides SE by √2 ≈ 1.41, not 2.
A smaller n makes the SE larger.
σ doesn’t enter how n scales: n × 4 regardless of σ.

questions.label: Q7
questions.prompt: 1% of people have a condition. A test catches 90% of cases and gives a false positive to 5% of healthy people. Given a positive test, the chance the person has the condition is about…

options.why: That’s P(+ | condition), the sensitivity, not P(condition | +).
That’s P(− | healthy). It ignores the low base rate.
That’s the prior. A positive test should raise it.
Forgot the C(5,2) = 10 ways to place the successes.
2/5 is a proportion, not a binomial probability.
That’s p for a single trial.
Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X) = 4·4. The constant shifts but doesn’t spread.
Var(aX + b) isn’t aVar(X) + b. Constants drop out, and a gets squared.
a must be squared: 2² × 4 = 16.
Adding 3 doesn’t change the spread, so drop the + 3.

questions.label: Q10
questions.prompt: Testing H₀: μ = 10 with n = 16, σ unknown. Which reference distribution?

options.why: σ is estimated by s, so use t with n − 1 df.
z needs a known σ (or a very large n).
One-sample t uses n − 1 = 15 df.
Chi-square is for variances/counts, not a mean.

questions.label: Q11
questions.prompt: Cov(x, y) = 6 and Var(x) = 3. The OLS slope of y on x is…

options.why: β̂₁ = Cov(x, y)/Var(x) = 6/3.
That’s Var(x)/Cov(x, y), upside down.
Multiplied instead of dividing.
Var(y) matters for r and R², not the slope.

questions.label: Q12
questions.prompt: Which change increases the power of a test (all else equal)?

options.why: The SE shrinks, so a real effect gives a larger test statistic.
A stricter α makes rejection harder, so power falls.
More noise means a bigger SE and lower power.
Smaller effects are harder to detect.
